rationale: B wins because it keeps the unknowns as unknowns; A gets too eager and starts printing the questions as facts. B's "Faire turns its wholesale marketplace into a lender for independent shops" is a clean, pitchable spine that asks "who carries the default risk" instead of pretending to know. A's "eat the credit risk itself" and "paying brands upfront out of its own pocket" are exactly how a founder gets walked into a reporter's follow-up they cannot answer.
gaps_in_A: "eat the credit risk itself" is not in the update. Faire underwrites the financing, but who bears the default loss is explicitly undisclosed.
"paying brands upfront out of its own pocket" invents the funding path, then the proof section admits it still needs to know whether this is Faire's balance sheet, a debt facility, or a bank partner.
"That makes a marketplace into a lender to 700,000 shops" treats marketplace size as product eligibility. A later question admits this may only apply to a subset, so the angle is overclaimed.
"credit provider Faire is displacing" manufactures an incumbent conflict. No bank, BNPL provider, factoring company, or displaced credit provider appears in the update.
gaps_in_B: "A $12.6B marketplace decides its next product is credit" is the thinnest angle; valuation is real, but the strategy story needs evidence that credit is a growth lever or revenue line.
"Story type: defensive-comment" is the wrong label for the brand angle. This is supplier economics or trade credit, not a defensive comment.

"cash-flow problem... can run any time in the next week or two" stretches the clock. With no outside retail data or seasonal peg supplied, this mostly lives on launch timing unless Faire brings real customer evidence.

"underwriting its own buyers on their order history rather than a bank score" is directionally fair, but still needs care; the update says order history, not what Faire replaces or excludes from underwriting.
